since1950.title: Lumen Gentium
since1950.summary: The Council's teaching on the Church: the Church as mystery and as People of God, the hierarchy with bishops forming a college with and under the Pope, the laity, the universal call to holiness, religious life, and Mary in the mystery of Christ and the Church. It restates existing dogma and defines nothing new.
since1950.continuity: Chapter 3 repeats Vatican I on the primacy and infallibility of the Pope and frames collegiality so that the college never acts without its head; the Preliminary Note of Explanation attached by order of Paul VI fixes that reading. Its description of who belongs to the Church builds on Mystici Corporis.

since1950.title: Dei Verbum
since1950.summary: Revelation, its transmission through Scripture and Tradition under the Magisterium, the inspiration and truth of Scripture, the Old and New Testaments, and Scripture in the life of the Church.
since1950.continuity: Restates Trent and Vatican I on the sources of revelation and the Church's role in interpreting them, and the inspiration of the whole canon. How its wording on Scripture's truth relates to Leo XIII and Benedict XV is discussed under inerrancy.

since1950.title: Sacrosanctum Concilium
since1950.summary: Principles for the reform of the liturgy: the liturgy as the work of Christ and the Church, full and active participation, revision of the rites, and a wider use of the vernacular while Latin is to be preserved in the Latin rites.
since1950.continuity: Trent condemned the claim that Mass must be in the vernacular only, while judging that vernacular celebration everywhere was not expedient at that time. Choosing the language of the rites is a disciplinary judgment the Church can revise, a power Trent itself affirms over the administration of the sacraments, provided their substance is kept.

since1950.title: Gaudium et Spes
since1950.summary: The Church in the modern world: human dignity, community, human activity, marriage and family, culture, economic and political life, war and peace. Its principles are authoritative teaching; many of its applications to circumstances are prudential.
since1950.continuity: Its teaching on marriage and procreation stands in line with Casti Connubii; its social teaching develops Leo XIII and Pius XI. The Council itself calls the constitution pastoral and notes that parts depend on changing circumstances.

since1950.title: Dignitatis Humanae
since1950.summary: Teaches that the human person has a right to immunity from coercion in religious matters, privately and publicly, within the just limits of public order, grounded in the dignity of the person. It states that it leaves untouched the traditional doctrine on the moral duty of individuals and societies toward the true religion and the one Church of Christ.
since1950.continuity: This is the flagship case for the hermeneutic of continuity. Pius IX condemned indifferentism and a supposed right to all manner of liberty; Leo XIII already taught that rulers may tolerate other worships for a great good. Dignitatis Humanae speaks of civil immunity, not a right to be in error.

since1950.title: Unitatis Redintegratio
since1950.summary: Catholic principles of ecumenism: the one Church of Christ, elements of sanctification and truth that exist outside its visible structure, and the conduct of dialogue with other Christians.
since1950.continuity: Holds that the fullness of the means of salvation is found in the Catholic Church, while recognizing real but imperfect communion with baptized Christians, in line with the older teaching on invincible ignorance and baptism.

since1950.title: Nostra Aetate
since1950.summary: The Church's relation to non-Christian religions: what is true and holy in them, esteem for Muslims, the spiritual bond with the Jewish people, rejection of the charge of collective Jewish guilt for the Passion, and condemnation of discrimination.
since1950.continuity: Does not deny that Christ is the one way of salvation or that the Church is necessary; it is read together with Florence and Pius IX on salvation and invincible ignorance.

since1950.title: Mysterium Fidei
since1950.summary: Reaffirms the Real Presence and transubstantiation against new theories that reduced the change in the Eucharist to a change of meaning or purpose alone.
since1950.continuity: Restates Trent's decree and canons on transubstantiation and insists that the Church's established terms keep their meaning.

since1950.title: Paenitemini
since1950.summary: Reorganizes the Church's penitential discipline: keeps the divine duty of penance while reducing and simplifying the days of fasting and abstinence and giving bishops' conferences room to adapt them.
since1950.continuity: The obligation to do penance is unchanged; only the ecclesiastical determination of how and when was revised.

since1950.title: Credo of the People of God
since1950.summary: A solemn profession of faith at the close of the Year of Faith, restating the Trinity, Christ, Mary, original sin, the Church, the Mass and transubstantiation, and the last things. Paul VI said it was not a dogmatic definition, though it repeats defined doctrine.
since1950.continuity: A compendium of the creeds and of defined teaching found throughout Denzinger.

since1950.title: Humanae Vitae
since1950.summary: Teaches that each marital act must remain open to the transmission of life and that direct contraception is intrinsically wrong, while permitting recourse to natural infertile periods for serious reasons.
since1950.continuity: Repeats Casti Connubii. Whether the teaching is also infallible by the ordinary universal magisterium is debated.

since1950.title: Missale Romanum
since1950.summary: Promulgates the revised Roman Missal prepared after the Council, with a new Order of Mass, more eucharistic prayers and a larger lectionary.
since1950.continuity: Rites are disciplinary and can be revised; the doctrine of the Mass as a true and proper sacrifice defined at Trent stands.

since1950.title: Ministeria Quaedam
since1950.summary: Suppresses first tonsure, the minor orders and the subdiaconate in the Latin Church and replaces them with the instituted ministries of lector and acolyte.
since1950.continuity: Trent taught that there are orders besides the priesthood, major and minor, but the number and form of the lower grades has always been ecclesiastical.

since1950.title: Mysterium Ecclesiae
since1950.kind: Declaration, Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: Defends the Church's unity, infallibility and the irreformability of definitions. It grants that dogmatic formulas are shaped by the language of their time and can be expressed more fully, while their meaning stays true and binding.
since1950.continuity: The modern Magisterium's own statement of the Vatican I rule that dogma keeps the same sense, and of the anti-Modernist insistence that dogmas do not evolve into other meanings.

since1950.title: Declaration on Procured Abortion
since1950.kind: Declaration, Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: Restates that direct abortion is gravely wrong from conception. A footnote leaves the philosophical question of the moment of ensoulment open, and the text argues that even a probable human life may not be taken.
since1950.continuity: Continues Innocent XI's condemnation of propositions that excused abortion before animation, and the Holy Office replies on direct killing of the fetus.

since1950.title: Inter Insigniores
since1950.kind: Declaration, Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: Explains why the Church does not consider herself authorized to admit women to priestly ordination: Christ's choice of men, the constant practice of the Church, and the priest's sacramental representation of Christ.
since1950.continuity: Sets out the reasons later confirmed as definitive in Ordinatio Sacerdotalis.

since1950.title: Familiaris Consortio
since1950.summary: The Christian family's role. Section 84 holds that the divorced and civilly remarried may not receive Communion unless they separate, or, where serious reasons prevent that, commit to living in complete continence.
since1950.continuity: Applies Trent's teaching on the indissolubility of marriage and the requirements of worthy Communion.

since1950.title: Code of Canon Law
since1950.summary: The revised code of law for the Latin Church, replacing the 1917 Code; it translates the Council's ecclesiology into law.
since1950.continuity: Law serves doctrine and can change; doctrinal content embedded in canons keeps its own weight.

since1950.title: Donum Veritatis
since1950.kind: Instruction, Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: On the vocation of the theologian. It distinguishes the assent owed to defined dogma, to definitive teaching, to authentic non-definitive teaching and to prudential interventions, and admits that some prudential documents may not be free of all deficiencies. It rejects organized public dissent.
since1950.continuity: The key text for sorting teaching by weight; it builds on Pius IX's teaching that Catholics are bound by more than defined dogma.

since1950.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church
since1950.summary: A full exposition of Catholic faith and morals for the universal Church, presented as a sure norm for teaching. Each statement keeps the weight of its sources; the Catechism itself does not raise or lower them.
since1950.continuity: Cites councils, popes and Fathers throughout. Its 2018 revision on the death penalty is the one text treated as a contested case.

since1950.title: Veritatis Splendor
since1950.summary: Fundamental moral theology: there are intrinsically evil acts that no intention or circumstance can justify; it rejects proportionalism and consequentialism and defends the link between freedom and truth.
since1950.continuity: Restates Trent on keeping the commandments with grace and the classical teaching on the object of the act.

since1950.title: Ordinatio Sacerdotalis
since1950.summary: Declares that the Church has no authority to confer priestly ordination on women and that this judgment is to be definitively held by all the faithful. A 1995 response of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith said the teaching belongs to the deposit of faith and is taught infallibly by the ordinary universal magisterium.
since1950.continuity: Confirms the Church's constant practice and the reasons given in Inter Insigniores.

since1950.title: Evangelium Vitae
since1950.summary: On the value of human life. In three solemn passages (57, 62, 65), invoking Petrine authority in communion with the bishops, the Pope confirms that the direct killing of the innocent, direct abortion and euthanasia are gravely immoral. It also narrows the cases in which the death penalty could be justified.
since1950.continuity: Confirms teaching found in Innocent XI's condemned propositions and the Holy Office replies on abortion; the death-penalty passages are continued in the Catechism revision of 2018.

since1950.title: Ut Unum Sint
since1950.summary: On ecumenism. It invites other Christians to help find a way of exercising the papal primacy that could serve unity, while affirming the primacy itself.
since1950.continuity: What it opens for discussion is the manner of exercise, not the defined substance of primacy and infallibility.

since1950.title: Ad Tuendam Fidem
since1950.kind: Apostolic letter (motu proprio) with doctrinal commentary
since1950.summary: Adds to canon law the duty to accept definitively proposed truths. The Congregation's accompanying commentary on the Profession of Faith sorts teaching into three tiers and gives examples of definitive truths: the male priesthood, the illicitness of euthanasia, prostitution and fornication, the legitimacy of papal elections and councils, canonizations, and the invalidity of Anglican orders.
since1950.continuity: Names Leo XIII's judgment on Anglican orders as a truth to be held definitively.

extra.label: Doctrinal commentary on the Profession of Faith

since1950.title: Common Christological Declaration with the Assyrian Church of the East
since1950.summary: John Paul II and Patriarch Mar Dinkha IV confess together that Christ is true God and true man, one person in two natures, and recognize the Catholic title Mother of God and the Assyrian title Mother of Christ as expressions of the same faith.
since1950.continuity: Measures the Assyrian tradition against Ephesus and Chalcedon rather than setting them aside.

since1950.title: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification
since1950.kind: Ecumenical agreement with the Lutheran World Federation
since1950.summary: Catholics and Lutherans state a consensus on basic truths of justification and say that the mutual condemnations of the sixteenth century do not apply to the other side's teaching as set out in the declaration. It is an agreement, not a magisterial definition.
since1950.continuity: The text itself says Trent's canons keep their force against what they condemn; the question is whether present Lutheran teaching is what they condemned.

since1950.title: Dominus Iesus
since1950.kind: Declaration, Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: On the unicity and salvific universality of Jesus Christ and the Church. It rejects relativist theologies of religion, teaches that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, and states that some of its content is to be held definitively.
since1950.continuity: Reaffirms the necessity of the Church for salvation in line with Florence and Pius IX, including the teaching on invincible ignorance.

since1950.title: Note on the Doctrinal Decrees concerning Antonio Rosmini
since1950.kind: Note, Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: Judges that the concerns behind the 1887 condemnation of forty propositions drawn from Rosmini can now be regarded as superseded, because read within his own system they do not carry the condemned meaning. The condemnation still holds for anyone who reads them in an idealist or ontologist sense.
since1950.continuity: A clear instance of a condemned proposition being judged in the sense intended; Rosmini was beatified in 2007.

since1950.title: Address to the Roman Curia
since1950.summary: Contrasts a hermeneutic of discontinuity and rupture with a hermeneutic of reform, of renewal in the continuity of the one subject Church, and uses religious liberty as the worked example: contingent historical applications changed while the principles remained.
since1950.continuity: Not a magisterial act in itself, but the classic statement of the reading this guide follows.

since1950.title: The Hope of Salvation for Infants Who Die Without Being Baptised
since1950.summary: Concludes that there are serious theological grounds to hope that unbaptized infants are saved, while noting that limbo remains a possible theological opinion and that this is a hope, not certain knowledge.
since1950.continuity: Pius VI condemned calling limbo a Pelagian fable; he did not define limbo. The study keeps baptism necessary and does not deny original sin.

since1950.title: Responses on Certain Aspects of the Doctrine on the Church
since1950.kind: Responses, Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: Answers five questions: Vatican II did not change the doctrine on the Church; subsists in means the Church of Christ continues to exist fully only in the Catholic Church; elements of the Church outside it are real; Orthodox churches are true particular churches though wounded; Protestant communities are ecclesial communities.
since1950.continuity: Reads Lumen Gentium 8 together with Mystici Corporis.

since1950.title: Summorum Pontificum
since1950.summary: Declares that the 1962 Missal was never juridically abrogated and permits its free use as an extraordinary form of the one Roman rite.
since1950.continuity: Treats the older and newer missals as two uses of one rite, expressing one faith.

since1950.title: Anglicanorum Coetibus
since1950.summary: Creates personal ordinariates for Anglican groups entering full communion, keeping elements of their liturgical and spiritual patrimony. Former Anglican clergy, including married men, may be ordained Catholic priests.
since1950.continuity: Their ordination as Catholic priests presupposes Leo XIII's judgment that Anglican orders are invalid.

since1950.title: Laudato Si'
since1950.summary: Care for creation and integral ecology. Its moral principles (stewardship, the universal destination of goods, the dignity of the poor) are authoritative teaching; its scientific and policy judgments are prudential, and the text itself says the Church does not settle scientific questions.
since1950.continuity: Develops the social teaching tradition on property and the common good.

since1950.title: Amoris Laetitia
since1950.summary: On love in the family. Chapter 8 discusses discernment for people in irregular unions and, in a footnote, mentions the help of the sacraments in certain cases. How far this changes Familiaris Consortio 84 is the central dispute.
since1950.continuity: A strict-continuity reading interprets chapter 8 in light of Trent on indissolubility, Familiaris Consortio 84 and Veritatis Splendor.

since1950.title: Revision of Catechism 2267 (death penalty)
since1950.kind: Rescript and letter of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: Rewrites the Catechism to say that, in light of the Gospel, the death penalty is inadmissible because it attacks the dignity of the person, and commits the Church to work for its abolition. The accompanying letter presents this as a development, not a contradiction.
since1950.continuity: Innocent III required the Waldensians to accept that civil power may impose death without mortal sin. A strict-continuity reading takes 2267 as a judgment about present conditions and the purposes of punishment.

since1950.title: Fratelli Tutti
since1950.summary: On fraternity and social friendship. It doubts that the just-war criteria can still be met given modern weapons, repeats opposition to the death penalty, and addresses migration and politics.
since1950.continuity: The just-war doctrine in the Catechism (2309) is not repealed; the encyclical's doubt about its present application is a prudential judgment.

since1950.title: Spiritus Domini
since1950.summary: Amends canon 230 so that women as well as men may be instituted as lectors and acolytes.
since1950.continuity: These are lay ministries rooted in baptism, not orders; the reservation of holy orders is untouched.

since1950.title: Traditionis Custodes
since1950.summary: Restricts use of the pre-1970 Roman liturgy, places it under the bishop's authority, and calls the reformed books the unique expression of the Roman rite's law of prayer.
since1950.continuity: A disciplinary reversal of Summorum Pontificum; neither document changes doctrine on the Mass.

since1950.title: Praedicate Evangelium
since1950.summary: Reorganizes the Roman Curia into dicasteries and allows lay members of the faithful to head them, grounding curial authority in delegation from the Pope.
since1950.continuity: Whether power of governance can be exercised without holy orders is a disputed question that this reform touches.

since1950.title: Fiducia Supplicans
since1950.kind: Declaration, Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: Allows brief, spontaneous, non-liturgical blessings of persons in irregular situations, including same-sex couples, while stating that the doctrine of marriage is unchanged and that no rite may resemble a wedding.
since1950.continuity: Its own text says it blesses persons, not unions. Several bishops' conferences declined to apply it.

since1950.title: Dignitas Infinita
since1950.kind: Declaration, Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: On human dignity, grounded in creation and redemption, with a list of grave violations including poverty, war, abortion, euthanasia, surrogacy, and the denial of sexual difference.
since1950.continuity: Restates the moral teaching of Evangelium Vitae and earlier condemnations of killing the innocent.

since1950.title: Dilexi Te
since1950.summary: Leo XIV's first major document, on love for the poor as central to the Gospel, drawing on Scripture, the Fathers, the saints and the social teaching tradition.
since1950.continuity: Continues the line from Leo XIII's social teaching.

since1950.title: Mater Populi Fidelis
since1950.kind: Doctrinal note, Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith
since1950.summary: On Marian titles about Mary's cooperation in salvation. It judges the title Co-redemptrix inappropriate and urges care with Mediatrix of all graces, while affirming Mary's real, subordinate cooperation in the work of her Son.
since1950.continuity: Neither title was ever defined. Leo XIII and Pius X used mediatrix language, which the note qualifies rather than rejects.

since1950.title: In Unitate Fidei
since1950.summary: Marks the 1700th anniversary of the Council of Nicaea and presents the Nicene faith in the divinity of Christ as the shared foundation of Christian unity.
since1950.continuity: Restates the Nicene and Nicene-Constantinopolitan creeds.

since1950.title: Report of the Petrocchi Commission on the female diaconate
since1950.summary: An advisory commission concluded that present historical and theological research rules out admitting women to the diaconate as a degree of holy orders, while saying this is not a definitive judgment like that on the priesthood and recommending further study.
since1950.continuity: Leaves the question open in principle; Ordinatio Sacerdotalis concerns the priesthood only.

disputed.title: Was Augustine’s account of concupiscence condemned at Trent?
disputed.question: How do Augustine’s remarks about the law of sin apply to second-first motions after a baptized person loses charity through mortal sin?
disputed.settled: Trent V.5 teaches that baptism truly remits the guilt of original sin and that the remaining inclination is called sin because it comes from sin and inclines to sin. Trent VI.7 describes justification as remission and interior renewal. VI.15 and canons 27–28 teach that mortal sin forfeits justifying grace, while faith may remain without charity.
disputed.open: Whether a particular second-first motion, here meaning an incipient movement with imperfect advertence or involvement of the will, involves any voluntary consent is a question about the act. Augustine’s terminology and the later scholastic classification must be compared with care.
disputed.reading: Contra Iulianum V.3.8 calls concupiscence sin, punishment of sin, and cause of sin. VI.16.49, 17.51 and 19.60–61 explain that baptism removes its guilt while the disorder remains. De nuptiis et concupiscentia I.23.25 distinguishes remaining concupiscence from the sin of consenting. After post-baptismal mortal sin, loss of charity deprives the will of its habitual ordering to God as supernatural end. Its conformity to the law of fleshly concupiscence describes this disordered orientation insofar as the will yields to it. Involuntary impulses remain distinct from culpable acts, and imperfect consent alone cannot establish a new mortal sin. The question concerns motions in the baptized who have lost charity. The standing inclination and the remitted guilt of original sin are distinct issues.

disputed.title: Cum occasione: five distinctions in reading Augustine
disputed.question: Which accounts of grace, freedom and redemption can an Augustinian affirm after Innocent X’s five censures?
disputed.settled: I. God’s commands can exceed unaided strength, while the just are not left without enabling help (De natura et gratia 43.50 and Trent VI.11). II. The efficacy of a particular divine aid is distinct from a universal denial that interior grace can be resisted (De correptione et gratia 8.17 and 12.33–34, read with Trent VI.5 and canon 4). III. The certainty of God’s efficacious action is distinct from a necessity that makes absence of external coercion the sole condition of freedom for merit and demerit (De gratia et libero arbitrio 16.32–17.33 and Trent VI, canon 4). IV. The beginning of faith itself is a gift. The possibility of resisting prevenient interior grace is compatible with that priority (De praedestinatione sanctorum 1.2–3.7 and Trent VI, canons 3–4). V. Christ’s death for all is distinct from the actual communication of its benefits (Trent VI.3). Augustine’s Enchiridion 103 offers a reading of 1 Timothy 2:4 about God’s saving will. It addresses a different question from whom Christ died for.
disputed.open: A passage supplied from Jansen’s Augustinus, tome II, book III, chapter 1, distinguishes having a power to act from having every aid needed for the act, then questions whether that sufficient aid is the true grace of Christ at issue. The edition, book heading, Latin wording and context need to be checked. Whether the aid Jansen concedes is genuinely interior, supernatural and resistible is the substantive question. Ad sacram attributes the condemned sense to Jansen. Comparing his exact formulations with the censured propositions remains a historical inquiry.
disputed.reading: A form of hypothetical universalism can pass the test of proposition V if it affirms that Christ truly died for everyone and distinguishes that universal scope from the particular application of the merits of his death. The fifth censure gives the note of heresy to restriction of Christ’s death for salvation to the predestined alone. Compatibility on this point leaves the model’s other claims about grace and freedom to be tested separately.

disputed.title: Grace and free will (Thomists and Molinists)
disputed.question: How does efficacious grace move the will without destroying its freedom?
disputed.settled: Grace is necessary for every salutary act, and the free will moved by God truly cooperates and can refuse (Trent).
disputed.open: Báñez attributes the infallible efficacy of a certain aid to divine motion and allows a different kind of interior aid to be refused. Molina says equal aids can receive different responses. His account of middle knowledge explains how God knows what a free person would do.
disputed.reading: Paul V closed the proceedings and forbade the disputants to censure each other. Innocent X disallows the circulating acts and the alleged condemnation of Molina. The comparison with Quesnel turns on the genuine power to dissent when moved by grace.

disputed.title: May we hope that all are saved?
disputed.question: Is it legitimate to hope that in fact no human being is damned?
disputed.settled: Hell exists and is eternal; those who die in actual mortal sin go there at once (Benedict XII). The doctrine that the punishment of the damned will end, and that all will be restored, was condemned.
disputed.open: The Church has never declared any individual to be in hell. Some theologians, notably Hans Urs von Balthasar, argued that one may hope all will be saved; critics answer that Scripture and the Fathers speak of the damned as real, and that such hope weakens the call to conversion.
disputed.reading: A teaching that all will certainly be saved is excluded. A prayerful hope for each person is common ground; whether one may hope that hell is in fact empty is debated among orthodox theologians.

disputed.title: Limbo of unbaptized infants
disputed.question: What happens to infants who die without baptism?
disputed.settled: Baptism is necessary for salvation, infants are to be baptized, and original sin is real and transmitted (Trent). Those who die with original sin alone do not enjoy the vision of God by their own claim (Innocent III, Florence). Pius VI condemned calling limbo a Pelagian fable.
disputed.open: Limbo itself was never defined. The International Theological Commission (2007) found serious grounds to hope these infants are saved by means known to God, while calling limbo a still-possible opinion.
disputed.reading: Pius VI condemned an accusation against a common opinion, not a denial of limbo as such. Both limbo and hope for these infants can be held without contradicting any definition.

disputed.title: When is the rational soul infused?
disputed.question: At conception, or at a later stage of development?
disputed.settled: Abortion is gravely wrong from conception. Innocent XI condemned the claims that abortion before animation is permitted and that it is probable the fetus lacks a rational soul until birth.
disputed.open: The precise moment of ensoulment. The 1974 Declaration on Procured Abortion expressly leaves that philosophical question open, and argues that even a probable human life may not be taken.
disputed.reading: The moral conclusion does not depend on the answer, so the question can remain open without weakening the teaching on abortion.

disputed.title: Evolution and the unity of the human race
disputed.question: How far may Catholics accept biological evolution and multiple first ancestors?
disputed.settled: The human soul is created directly by God. Original sin comes from a real sin of Adam and is passed to all (Trent). Pius XII allowed research on the evolution of the body.
disputed.open: Pius XII said polygenism could not be held because it was not apparent how it could be reconciled with the doctrine of original sin. Later theologians have proposed ways to reconcile a large early population with a single first couple or a single original sin; none has been approved or condemned.
disputed.reading: The fixed point is original sin as a real event at the origin of humanity and passed on to all; models that keep that are argued for in good faith, and the question is not closed.

disputed.title: Mary as Mediatrix of all graces
disputed.question: Is every grace given through Mary's intercession, and should this be defined?
disputed.settled: Mary cooperated in a unique, subordinate way in the work of her Son, and Christ is the one mediator.
disputed.open: Leo XIII and Pius X used mediatrix language, and there were twentieth-century movements for a definition. The 2025 note Mater Populi Fidelis urges care with the title and rules out any sense that would make Mary a source of grace alongside Christ.
disputed.reading: An undefined pious teaching, held in a sense subordinate to Christ's mediation. Its future definition is not expected.

disputed.title: Could a pope teach heresy as a private person?
disputed.question: What happens if a pope, not speaking ex cathedra, teaches something heretical?
disputed.settled: The Pope is infallible when he defines a doctrine of faith or morals ex cathedra under the conditions Vatican I set out.
disputed.open: Whether a pope can fall into personal heresy, and what would follow, was argued by Bellarmine, Cajetan, Suárez and John of St. Thomas, who reached different answers. The case of Honorius is the usual historical test. The old canonists' exception (Gratian, D. 40 c. 6: the pope is judged by no one "unless he is found to have strayed from the faith") and the deposition of Gregory VI at Sutri in 1046 are the usual historical starting points; see the question on Sutri.
disputed.reading: Vatican I's definition is limited by its conditions, so the question it leaves untouched remains a matter for theologians and canonists.

disputed.title: The scope of biblical inerrancy
disputed.question: Is Scripture free from error in everything it asserts, or only in matters touching salvation?
disputed.settled: All of Scripture is inspired and has God as author (Trent, Vatican I). Leo XIII and Benedict XV rejected restricting inspiration or inerrancy to faith and morals.
disputed.open: Dei Verbum 11 speaks of the truth God wanted put in Scripture for the sake of our salvation. Some read this as limiting inerrancy to salvific matters; others read it as describing the purpose of the whole truth of Scripture without limiting it.
disputed.reading: The continuity reading takes the phrase as qualifying the kind of truth, not the extent of inerrancy, since an explicit reversal of Leo XIII and Benedict XV is not stated. Attention to literary genres (Pius XII) settles many apparent errors.

disputed.title: Women and the diaconate
disputed.question: Can women receive the diaconate as a degree of holy orders?
disputed.settled: Priestly ordination is reserved to men, to be held definitively (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis).
disputed.open: Ordinatio Sacerdotalis addresses the priesthood only. Francis set up two study commissions (2016 and 2020). A summary of the second, chaired by Cardinal Petrocchi, was released by Leo XIV in December 2025: it concluded against admitting women to the diaconate as a degree of holy orders, but said explicitly that this was not a definitive judgment.
disputed.reading: Current judgment is negative but not definitive; historical deaconesses are generally judged not to have received the same sacrament as deacons.

disputed.title: Pope Honorius I and monothelitism
disputed.question: Did Honorius teach the heresy of one will in Christ?
disputed.settled: Constantinople III defines two natural wills and operations in Christ. It rejects Honorius’s correspondence and says he confirmed Sergius’s impious doctrines. Leo II confirms the anathema.
disputed.open: John IV understood Honorius to mean that Christ had no divided or sinful human will. Leo’s letter to Spain describes negligence. The printed Latin and Greek of the confirmation differ in their description of Honorius’s agency.
disputed.reading: The letters instruct bishops on a controversy. Their purpose and addressees give no evidence of a definition binding the whole Church under the criteria in Pastor aeternus.

disputed.title: Pope Liberius and the Arian crisis
disputed.question: Did Liberius sign a semi-Arian formula while in exile?
disputed.settled: Anastasius I counted Liberius among those who suffered exile for the Nicene faith.
disputed.open: Some ancient sources say he signed an ambiguous creed at Sirmium under duress to return to Rome; the authenticity of the letters involved is disputed. During his exile the emperor Constantius had Felix II installed at Rome; the Annuario Pontificio lists Felix as an antipope, though a later cult honoured him as a martyr pope.
disputed.reading: Even on the hostile account, a signature under coercion is not a definition binding the Church.

disputed.title: Jansen's five propositions: the question of fact
disputed.question: Can the Church judge that a book actually teaches a condemned sense?
disputed.settled: Innocent X condemned five propositions; Alexander VII declared they are taken from Jansen's Augustinus and condemned in his sense; Clement XI ruled that respectful silence does not satisfy the obedience owed.
disputed.open: The historical relation of the wording of the propositions to the book and the precise theological grade of this particular judgment. The 1998 commentary gives examples of definitive judgments connected to revelation by historical necessity.
disputed.reading: Alexander VII attributed the condemned sense to Jansenius. Clement XI then required the faithful to reject that sense sincerely in word and heart.

disputed.title: Michael du Bay (Baius): the 79 propositions
disputed.question: What was censured about concupiscence and the gratuity of grace?
disputed.settled: Pius V condemns the propositions under several censures applied respectively. Trent says that concupiscence remains after baptism and cannot harm those who withhold consent and resist with Christ’s grace.
disputed.open: The Comma Pianum affects whether the strict and proper sense specifies the censure or the concession about possible defenses. The bull gives no individual censure for propositions 74 or 75.
disputed.reading: Proposition 75 calls the felt impulse a transgression while denying imputation as sin. Proposition 21 makes participation in divine nature due to original integrity. Case A5 tests these distinct claims against Trent and Humani generis.

disputed.title: Meister Eckhart: the 28 articles
disputed.question: Is Eckhart's mystical language heretical?
disputed.settled: John XXII condemned 17 articles as heretical and 11 others as evil-sounding, rash and suspect of heresy.
disputed.open: The lesser censure on the eleven implies that with explanation they could bear a Catholic sense. Eckhart had declared before his death that he retracted anything that could be read in a heretical sense.
disputed.reading: The graded censures show that the bull did not judge every article equally. His language remains open to orthodox interpretation where it is not one of the heretical articles in its condemned sense.

disputed.title: Quesnel: the 101 propositions of Unigenitus
disputed.question: What did Clement XI censure in propositions that echo Augustine or commend Scripture reading?
disputed.settled: Clement XI condemned all 101 propositions with censures applied respectively. The bull especially names renewals of Jansenius’s propositions in the sense already condemned. It also condemns Quesnel’s book.
disputed.open: The bull gives no individual notes. Gres-Gayer reports that Clement initially suspended judgment on proposition 13. It remained in the promulgated list. The precise grounds for that censure and the one on proposition 80 remain open in this review.
disputed.reading: A sentence may have an orthodox sense in isolation and carry a censurable implication in a particular gloss or argument. For proposition 13, the efficacy of a particular saving aid and a denial of all resistance to interior grace are distinct claims. For proposition 80, the general encouragement of Scripture reading and the exclusion of ecclesial oversight are distinct claims. Quesnel’s defense distinguishes effects of grace, and his gloss on Acts 8 appeals to the Church’s teachers. Those texts complicate the proposed adverse readings. Case A3 examines the evidence, and the bull itself does not assign either proposition an individual rationale.

disputed.title: Fénelon and pure love
disputed.question: Was the ideal of disinterested love of God condemned?
disputed.settled: Innocent XII condemned 23 propositions from Fénelon's Maxims of the Saints, in their obvious sense or in the sense of the opinions connected with them.
disputed.open: Fénelon submitted at once. Loving God for himself, above all and without self-seeking, remains the teaching of the saints.
disputed.reading: What was condemned is the claim that a perfect soul can give up the hope of salvation as a motive, not the primacy of charity.

disputed.title: Antonio Rosmini: the forty propositions
disputed.question: Do the forty propositions condemned in 1887 express Rosmini's teaching?
disputed.settled: The propositions are condemned in an idealist or ontologist sense contrary to the faith.
disputed.open: Nothing remains doctrinally open: the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith judged in 2001 that the concerns behind the decree are superseded when the texts are read within his system.
disputed.reading: An explicit modern ruling that a condemned proposition and an author's true meaning can differ. Rosmini was beatified in 2007.

disputed.title: Luther's proposition 33: burning heretics
disputed.question: Did Leo X teach that burning heretics is God's will?
disputed.settled: Exsurge Domine condemned 41 propositions respectively as heretical, scandalous, false, offensive to pious ears or misleading, without assigning censures one by one.
disputed.open: Which censure applies to proposition 33 was never specified, and it may be among the lighter ones.
disputed.reading: The usual reading is that the condemnation defended the Church's right to impose penalties, a right Luther denied, not burning as such. John Paul II later asked forgiveness for the use of violence in the service of truth, and Dignitatis Humanae excludes coercion of conscience.

disputed.title: Pistoia and the vernacular liturgy
disputed.question: What did Pius VI censure in Pistoia’s proposal for public worship?
disputed.settled: Pistoia proposed a bilingual ritual and manual. Pius VI censured the charge of acting against apostolic practice and God’s designs as applied to bringing the vernacular into liturgical prayers.
disputed.open: The practical use intended for the local ritual and manual needs further documentary evidence. Proposition 67 addresses a separate claim about the obligation to read Scripture.
disputed.reading: Trent rejects an exclusive obligation to say Mass in the vernacular. Vatican II retains Latin and permits a wider use of the vernacular under competent authority.

disputed.title: Syllabus 80: progress, liberalism and modern civilization
disputed.question: Does the Church reject all modern progress?
disputed.settled: Pius IX condemned the proposition that the Pope can and should reconcile himself with progress, liberalism and modern civilization.
disputed.open: Every Syllabus proposition must be read in the source it cites. Proposition 80 comes from the 1861 allocution Iamdudum cernimus, which used these words for the anticlerical program of the time.
disputed.reading: Condemned is reconciliation with that program, not with genuine progress, which Gaudium et Spes and the social encyclicals welcome.

disputed.title: Americanism
disputed.question: Were American Catholics condemned for heresy?
disputed.settled: Leo XIII rejected the opinions that the Church should soften doctrine to win converts, that external guidance is less needed under the Spirit, and that active virtues outrank passive ones.
disputed.open: Leo said he was not condemning the American Church or its legitimate customs. Cardinal Gibbons replied that no educated American Catholic held the opinions described.
disputed.reading: A condemnation of opinions as described, binding on anyone who holds them, but historians often call it a phantom heresy.

disputed.status: Definition limited to its final sentence
disputed.title: Unam Sanctam and the two swords
disputed.question: Is the whole of Boniface VIII's bull, including the temporal power of the Pope over kings, defined?
disputed.settled: The final sentence declares that subjection to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation for every human creature.
disputed.open: The argument about spiritual and temporal swords is the reasoning of the bull, which theologians commonly do not count as part of the definition.
disputed.reading: The defined sentence repeats the teaching on the necessity of the Church (compare Florence), read with the doctrine of invincible ignorance.

disputed.status: Formula accepted in an orthodox sense
disputed.title: The Filioque and the Greek formula
disputed.question: Do the Latin "and the Son" and the Greek "through the Son" contradict each other?
disputed.settled: The Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son as from one principle (Lyons II, Florence).
disputed.open: Florence accepted that the Greek Fathers' formula "from the Father through the Son" expresses the same faith. Eastern Catholics recite the creed without the Filioque.
disputed.reading: A formula condemned in one sense can be the Church's own in another; what matters is the sense, not the wording.

disputed.status: Formula accepted in an orthodox sense
disputed.title: "One nature of the Word incarnate" and the Eastern churches
disputed.question: Can churches that reject Chalcedon's wording hold the Chalcedonian faith?
disputed.settled: Christ is one person in two natures, without confusion or separation (Chalcedon).
disputed.open: Constantinople II itself accepts Cyril's phrase "one nature of the Word made flesh" in the sense the Fathers meant. Common declarations with Oriental Orthodox and Assyrian churches since 1973 build on that.
disputed.reading: Agreement in faith under different formulas, judged by the sense; the definitions of Ephesus and Chalcedon stay the measure.

disputed.title: Outside the Church no salvation
disputed.question: How do Florence and Vatican II fit together?
disputed.settled: Florence requires union with the Church before death. The Holy Office in 1949 explains that actual incorporation as a member and union by desire are distinct. In invincible ignorance that desire can be implicit.
disputed.open: How the saving grace of Christ reaches persons who have not heard the Gospel and how supernatural faith is present in those cases.
disputed.reading: The Holy Office requires that the desire be formed by perfect charity and that implicit desire be accompanied by supernatural faith. Lumen Gentium cites the letter in its account of those who have yet to receive the Gospel.

disputed.title: Usury and modern interest
disputed.question: The Church condemned profit on loans. Why is interest accepted now?
disputed.settled: Taking profit from a loan by reason of the loan itself is unjust (Benedict XIV, Vix pervenit).
disputed.open: How far extrinsic titles (lost profit, risk, the productive use of money in a market economy) justify interest. Lateran V had already approved modest charges by the Mountains of Piety.
disputed.reading: The principle stands; what changed is the economic reality of money and credit, which makes titles to compensation ordinary. Exploitative lending remains condemned.

disputed.title: The Biblical Commission decrees (1905–1915)
disputed.question: Must Catholics hold Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch, the historicity of Genesis 1–3 as decreed, and the authenticity of the Johannine Comma?
disputed.settled: Facts touching the foundations of the faith (creation, the unity of the human race, original sin) are to be held. Pius X required obedience to the Commission's decisions.
disputed.open: The 1927 Holy Office clarification allowed scholars to examine the Comma; in 1955 the Commission's own secretaries said the early decrees retain force only where they touch faith and morals. The Commission was later restructured as an advisory body.
disputed.reading: These were prudential safeguards in a crisis, not definitions; where they touch doctrine they still bind, elsewhere scholarship is free.

disputed.title: The Pisan popes and the deposition of John XXIII
disputed.question: Were Alexander V and John XXIII true popes, and did Constance validly depose John XXIII?
disputed.settled: Martin V was the one certain pope from 1417, and his election ended the schism. The Annuario Pontificio lists the Roman line (Gregory XII) as legitimate, and Alexander V and John XXIII as antipopes; Angelo Roncalli took the name John XXIII in 1958.
disputed.open: The Church never defined which line was legitimate between 1378 and 1417; the Roman list is a historical judgment, revised as late as the twentieth century, and the popes who later took the names Alexander VI and VII counted Alexander V. Martin V's own register calls Alexander V "our predecessor" and says John XXIII "succeeded him in the papacy" and was deposed "from the papacy" (C10), and his bull of session 42 calls the deposition "canonical" (C8). Gregory XII, for his part, convoked the council before resigning (C2), which on the Roman reading is what gave it authority. Other documents of Martin V's pontificate are more guarded: the Synod of Tortosa (1429), under his legate, says the deposed claimants lost the right "they claimed to have," and that Gregory XII renounced "whatever right belonged to him" (C15).
disputed.reading: Constance ended the schism on any reading: if the Roman line was legitimate, Gregory XII convoked the council and resigned; if the Pisan line was, John XXIII had convoked it and was deposed after he fled it, a deposition Martin V called canonical. Either way Martin V's election is certain and the acts that produced it were confirmed by him. Martin's chancery language shows how Constance itself saw the Pisan popes; it does not settle the historical question, which remains open to argument.

disputed.title: Religious liberty
disputed.question: Does Dignitatis Humanae contradict Quanta Cura and the Syllabus?
disputed.settled: Indifferentism is condemned; there is a moral duty to seek and embrace the true religion. Dignitatis Humanae says it leaves that traditional doctrine untouched.
disputed.open: Whether a civil right to immunity from coercion is compatible with the nineteenth-century condemnations. Some see a real change of teaching; traditionalist critics see a rupture; others see development.
disputed.reading: The earlier texts condemned a supposed right to error and the separation of morality from religion. Dignitatis Humanae teaches civil immunity within public order and keeps the duty toward the truth. Leo XIII already allowed tolerance of other worships for the common good. Benedict XVI chose this as his example of reform in continuity.

disputed.title: "Subsists in" (Lumen Gentium 8)
disputed.question: Did Vatican II stop identifying the Church of Christ with the Catholic Church?
disputed.settled: There is one Church of Christ; Pius XII taught that the Mystical Body is the Catholic Church.
disputed.open: Why the Council wrote subsists in instead of is. Some read it as allowing the Church of Christ to exist elsewhere.
disputed.reading: The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (2007) says it means the Church of Christ continues to exist fully only in the Catholic Church, while acknowledging elements of the Church outside its visible bounds.

disputed.title: Collegiality and the primacy
disputed.question: Does the college of bishops share supreme power in a way that limits the Pope?
disputed.settled: The Pope has full, supreme and universal power that he can always exercise freely (Vatican I).
disputed.open: Lumen Gentium 22 says the college with its head is also a subject of supreme power. Theologians debate whether there are one or two subjects of supreme power.
disputed.reading: The Preliminary Note of Explanation, added by order of Paul VI, says the college never acts without its head and that the Pope's power is untouched. That is the authoritative key.

disputed.title: The death penalty
disputed.question: Is the death penalty now taught to be wrong in itself?
disputed.settled: Innocent III required the Waldensians to accept that civil power may impose death without mortal sin. The Catechism of 1992/1997 restricted it to cases of absolute necessity.
disputed.open: The 2018 revision calls it inadmissible because it attacks the dignity of the person. Whether that states an absolute moral norm or a judgment about present conditions is disputed.
disputed.reading: Read strictly in continuity, 2267 cannot mean the penalty is intrinsically evil, since that would contradict earlier teaching. It is taken as a judgment that today it is not needed and does not serve the purposes of punishment.

disputed.title: Amoris Laetitia and Communion for the remarried
disputed.question: May the divorced and civilly remarried living as spouses receive Communion?
disputed.settled: Marriage is indissoluble (Trent). Some acts are intrinsically evil (Veritatis Splendor). Familiaris Consortio 84 required separation or continence.
disputed.open: Chapter 8 and footnote 351 suggest sacramental help in some cases; the Buenos Aires bishops' guidelines, approved by Francis and published in the Acta Apostolicae Sedis, allow access in some situations. Four cardinals' dubia (2016) asking how this fits earlier teaching were not answered formally.
disputed.reading: A strict-continuity reading interprets Amoris Laetitia by Familiaris Consortio and Veritatis Splendor and takes subjective culpability as relevant to guilt, not to the objective norm.

disputed.title: Fiducia Supplicans and blessings
disputed.question: Do blessings of couples in irregular situations imply approval of their unions?
disputed.settled: Marriage is between a man and a woman; the Church cannot bless sinful unions (2021 response of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith).
disputed.open: Fiducia Supplicans allows short non-liturgical blessings of persons who are in such couples. Several bishops' conferences declined to apply it; the Dicastery issued a clarifying press note in January 2024.
disputed.reading: Read strictly, the blessing is of persons asking help to live by God's will, not of the union, and the doctrine of marriage is unchanged, as the document itself states.

disputed.title: Is Humanae Vitae infallible?
disputed.question: Is the teaching on contraception definitive?
disputed.settled: Direct contraception is gravely wrong (Casti Connubii, Humanae Vitae, the Catechism).
disputed.open: Some theologians, notably John Ford and Germain Grisez, argued it is infallibly taught by the ordinary universal magisterium; others hold it is authoritative but not infallible.
disputed.reading: Either way it requires at least religious submission of mind and will; nothing in later teaching has softened it.

disputed.title: Is Ordinatio Sacerdotalis infallible?
disputed.question: Is the reservation of priesthood to men infallibly taught?
disputed.settled: John Paul II declared it to be held definitively; the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (1995) said it is taught infallibly by the ordinary universal magisterium.
disputed.open: Some theologians argue the criteria for that kind of infallibility were not shown to be met.
disputed.reading: Under the 1998 commentary it is a definitive truth requiring firm assent.

disputed.title: Mary as Co-redemptrix
disputed.question: Is the title Co-redemptrix legitimate?
disputed.settled: Mary cooperated uniquely, by grace, in the redemption won by Christ alone.
disputed.open: Some popes and saints used the term; there was a movement for a definition. Mater Populi Fidelis (2025) judges the title inappropriate because it can obscure Christ's unique mediation.
disputed.reading: The title was never defined, so declining it changes no doctrine; the reality it intended (Mary's subordinate cooperation) is reaffirmed.

disputed.title: Trent and the Joint Declaration on Justification
disputed.question: Do Trent's anathemas still apply to Lutheran teaching?
disputed.settled: Trent's canons on justification remain in force against what they condemn; the Joint Declaration says so too.
disputed.open: The declaration claims the condemnations do not touch Lutheran teaching as presented in it. The Catholic Church's official response (1998) noted continuing difficulties, especially on whether the justified are at once righteous and sinners.
disputed.reading: An ecumenical judgment about what each side now teaches, not a change in Trent's doctrine.

disputed.title: The reformed Mass, Summorum Pontificum and Traditionis Custodes
disputed.question: Did the liturgical reform change doctrine, and what is the status of the older Mass?
disputed.settled: The Mass is a true sacrifice (Trent); the Church may change rites while keeping the substance of the sacraments.
disputed.open: How the two forms relate: Benedict XVI said the older missal was never abrogated, while Francis called the reformed books the unique expression of the Roman rite. Pius V's perpetual clause in Quo primum is a disciplinary formula that later popes have always been free to revise.
disputed.reading: Both popes acted in the disciplinary sphere; neither altered doctrine on the Mass.

disputed.title: Communion under both kinds
disputed.question: Councils restricted the chalice. Why is it offered again?
disputed.settled: Christ is wholly received under either species, and the Church may decide how Communion is distributed (Constance, Trent).
disputed.open: Nothing doctrinal. Trent left the question of granting the chalice to the Pope.
disputed.reading: Constance and Trent condemned the claim that both kinds are necessary for salvation, not the practice itself.

disputed.title: Other changed disciplines
disputed.question: Which post-conciliar changes are purely disciplinary?
disputed.settled: Ecclesiastical law and rites can be changed by competent authority; divine law cannot.
disputed.open: Prudence of particular changes: reduced fasting and abstinence (1966), the one-hour Eucharistic fast (1964), Communion in the hand by indult (1969), suppression of minor orders and the subdiaconate (1972), female altar servers (1994), women as instituted lectors and acolytes (2021), married former Anglican clergy (2009). Clerical celibacy in the Latin Church is itself a discipline, attested since the Council of Elvira.
disputed.reading: Each can be judged on its merits without touching faith; reasoned disagreement is legitimate.

disputed.title: Can laypeople exercise power of governance?
disputed.question: May a layperson head a curial office and exercise authority over clergy?
disputed.settled: Lumen Gentium 21 teaches that episcopal consecration confers the offices of teaching and governing as well as sanctifying.
disputed.open: Praedicate Evangelium (2022) allows laypeople to head dicasteries by papal delegation. Canonists divide over whether governance power derives from orders or can be delegated by the Pope's jurisdiction alone.
disputed.reading: Read in continuity, lay officials act by delegated papal authority, not by power of their own, leaving the sacramental basis of the bishops' office intact.

disputed.title: Prudential judgments in recent social teaching
disputed.question: How binding are papal statements on climate, war, weapons and migration?
disputed.settled: Moral principles (the dignity of the person, the common good, the universal destination of goods, the just-war criteria) bind as authoritative teaching.
disputed.open: Applications are prudential: the scientific claims of Laudato Si', Fratelli Tutti's doubt that any modern war can be just, Francis's condemnation of possessing nuclear weapons, and specific migration and economic policies.
disputed.reading: Donum Veritatis §24 admits that prudential interventions may contain deficiencies. Catholics owe them serious, respectful consideration but may reasonably disagree on the application.

threads.title: The Trinity
threads.summary: From the Nicene homoousios to the Council of Florence: one God in three persons, each fully God, distinct only by their relations of origin.

steps.note: Nicaea: the Son is of one substance with the Father, against Arius.
Constantinople I: the Holy Spirit is Lord and giver of life, adored and glorified with the Father and the Son.
Damasus's synod: the Holy Spirit is truly God, of the divine substance, like the Son.
The Athanasian Creed: unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, persons not confused, substance not divided.
Toledo XI: a full Latin confession of the Trinity, persons distinguished by relation.
Lateran IV: one supreme reality, Father, Son and Spirit; against Joachim's account of the divine unity (n. 431).
Lyons II: the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle.
Florence: the Greek "through the Son" means the same faith as the Latin "and the Son."
Florence, for the Jacobites: in God all is one except where there is opposition of relation.
Leo XIV marks 1700 years of Nicaea and presents its faith as the ground of Christian unity.

threads.title: Christ, true God and true man
threads.summary: The councils from Ephesus to Constantinople III fix the confession of one person in two natures with two wills, and later ecumenical agreements measure other traditions by it.

steps.note: Ephesus receives Cyril's letter: the Word united flesh to himself hypostatically.
Ephesus: Mary is Mother of God, because the one she bore is God the Word made flesh.
Leo's Tome: each nature keeps its properties, joined in one person.
Chalcedon: one and the same Christ in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation.
Constantinople II: Cyril's "one nature of the Word made flesh" is accepted only in the Fathers' sense.
Honorius writes ambiguously of one will (the case later debated, see the disputed questions).
Constantinople III: two natural wills and two operations, the human will following the divine.
Lateran IV: the Son incarnate by the whole Trinity, true God and true man.
1994: the Assyrian Church of the East and Rome confess the same faith under different titles for Mary.

threads.title: Mary
threads.summary: From Mother of God to the Assumption, with the Immaculate Conception moving from permitted opinion to dogma, and titles of mediation left undefined.

steps.note: Ephesus: Theotokos, Mother of God, defended against Nestorius.
Siricius: Mary's virginity after the birth of Christ.
Lateran Synod of 649: Mary ever-virgin, conceiving without seed and giving birth without corruption.
Sixtus IV approves a feast of the Immaculate Conception while the question is still debated.
Sixtus IV forbids each side to call the other heretical.
Trent declines to include Mary in its decree on original sin.
Alexander VII describes the belief in her preservation from original sin from the first instant.
Pius IX defines the Immaculate Conception (1854).
Leo XIII: Mary as mediatrix to the Mediator, in a subordinate sense.
Pius XII defines the Assumption (1950), the last dogma defined.
Lumen Gentium 8 places Mary within the mystery of Christ and the Church.
2025: Co-redemptrix judged inappropriate; Mary's subordinate cooperation reaffirmed.

threads.title: Primacy and infallibility of the Pope
threads.summary: From Clement's letter to Corinth to Vatican I's definitions, and the post-conciliar discussion of how the primacy is exercised.

steps.note: Clement of Rome intervenes in the church of Corinth.
Serdica: bishops may appeal to the bishop of Rome.
Siricius: Peter bears the burdens of all in his successor.
Innocent I: matters from all provinces are referred to the Apostolic See.
Boniface I: what Rome has decided may not be reopened.
At Ephesus the papal legate: Peter lives and judges in his successors.
Unam Sanctam: subjection to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation.
Constance, amid three rival claimants, asserts authority over anyone "even if papal" (Haec Sancta); its standing is disputed.
Florence: the Pope has primacy over the whole world and full power to rule the Church.
Florence condemns Basel's claim that a council's superiority over the pope is a truth of faith.
Pius II forbids appeals from the pope to a future council.
Lateran V: the pope alone convokes, transfers and dissolves councils.
Vatican I: the primacy of jurisdiction is immediate and episcopal over all the faithful.
Vatican I: the Pope's power is full and supreme, not merely supervision.
Vatican I defines papal infallibility and its conditions.
Lumen Gentium repeats Vatican I and sets collegiality under and with the head.
John Paul II invites discussion of the exercise, not the substance, of the primacy.

threads.title: Scripture and Tradition
threads.summary: The canon, the two channels of revelation, inspiration and inerrancy, and the Church's authority to interpret.

steps.note: Damasus's council lists the canon of Scripture.
Carthage gives the same canon.
Trent: the Gospel comes in written books and unwritten traditions, both received with equal reverence; the canon fixed.
Trent: no one may interpret Scripture against the Church's sense or the consent of the Fathers.
Vatican I: the books are sacred because written under the Spirit's inspiration with God as author.
Leo XIII: inspiration excludes error from the whole of Scripture.
Pius X requires obedience to the Biblical Commission's decisions.
Benedict XV rejects limiting inerrancy to religious matters.
Pius XII: the interpreter must attend to the literary forms of the ancient writers.
Dei Verbum restates the doctrine and speaks of the truth recorded for our salvation.

threads.title: Grace and justification
threads.summary: From the African councils against Pelagius to Trent's decree, the Jansenist condemnations, and the Joint Declaration with Lutherans.

steps.note: Carthage: grace helps us not to sin, not only forgives past sins.
Carthage: without grace we can do nothing, not merely do good with more difficulty.
The Indiculus: God is the author of every good disposition, and free choice is set free, not destroyed.
Orange II: free will weakened in Adam is repaired only by the grace of baptism.
Trent: the beginning of justification is from prevenient grace, with free cooperation.
Trent's canons on justification, from the first against Pelagianism to the last against misreadings of the decree.
Paul V: Thomists and Molinists may each teach their view on efficacious grace.
Innocent X condemns Jansen's first proposition: some commandments impossible to the just.
Clement XI condemns Quesnel's claim that no grace is given outside the Church.
1999: Catholics and Lutherans state a consensus on basic truths of justification.

threads.title: Original sin and the unity of the human race
threads.summary: The doctrine defended against Pelagius, defined at Trent, and kept as the fixed point in modern questions about evolution and unbaptized infants.

steps.note: Carthage: Adam was not made subject to death by nature but by sin.
Carthage: infants are baptized for the remission of sin they contract from Adam.
Orange II: Adam's sin passed death and sin to the whole human race.
Trent: Adam's transgression harmed his posterity, transmitting sin and death.
Trent: newborn infants are to be baptized for the remission of original sin.
Pius VI rejects calling limbo a Pelagian fable.
Pius XII permits research on the evolution of the human body.
Pius XII: polygenism cannot be held while it is not apparent how it fits original sin.
2007: a theological study on hope for unbaptized infants.

threads.title: The Eucharist
threads.summary: Real presence, transubstantiation and sacrifice, from Berengarius to Trent and Paul VI.

steps.note: Berengarius's oath: bread and wine are substantially changed into Christ's body and blood.
Lateran IV: the bread and wine are transubstantiated.
Constance condemns Wycliffe's claim that the substance of bread remains.
Constance defends communion under one kind for the laity.
Trent: Christ is truly, really and substantially contained under the species.
Trent: the change is fittingly and properly called transubstantiation.
Trent: the Church may change how sacraments are administered, preserving their substance.
Trent: the Mass is a true and proper sacrifice.
The Holy Office judges a proposed philosophical account of transubstantiation intolerable.
Paul VI reaffirms transubstantiation against theories of mere change of meaning.
The revised Missal changes the rites, not the doctrine of the Mass.

threads.title: Penance and confession
threads.summary: From private confession under Leo the Great to the annual precept and Trent's canons, and reconciliation of the dying.

steps.note: Innocent I: penance and communion for the dying.
Celestine I: penance must not be refused to the dying who ask for it.
Leo the Great: secret confession to priests suffices; public reading of sins is forbidden.
Lateran IV: every Catholic confesses at least once a year.
Florence: the matter and form of penance.
Trent: confession of all mortal sins is of divine law.
Trent: penance is truly and properly a sacrament.
Trent: sacramental confession is instituted by divine law and necessary for salvation.
Paul VI reorganizes penitential practice while keeping the duty of penance.

threads.title: Marriage
threads.summary: Indissolubility, sacramentality and the ends of marriage, and the post-conciliar questions about Communion and blessings.

steps.note: Elvira: a woman who leaves an adulterous husband may not remarry while he lives.
Innocent III's profession for the Waldensians affirms that marriage is lawful and good.
Florence: marriage is the seventh sacrament, sign of Christ and the Church.
Trent: the Church does not err in teaching that adultery does not dissolve the bond.
Leo XIII, Arcanum: the Church's authority over Christian marriage.
Pius XI, Casti Connubii: marriage instituted and restored by God, not by man.
Casti Connubii: any use of marriage deliberately frustrated of its power to procreate is grave sin.
Casti Connubii against divorce.
Humanae Vitae repeats the teaching on contraception.
Familiaris Consortio 84 on the divorced and remarried.
Amoris Laetitia, chapter 8, and the dispute over its reading.
Fiducia Supplicans: blessings of persons, with the doctrine of marriage restated.

threads.title: The Church and salvation
threads.summary: From Pelagius II and Lateran IV to Florence, Pius IX on invincible ignorance, and Vatican II's teaching on the Church.

steps.note: Pelagius II: one slain outside the Church cannot attain its rewards.
